reason: Ranked at 6:1 and again at 6:7 on the Book of Mormon's standing way of locating a congregation ('the church which was established in the city of Zarahemla', 'the church which was in the city of Zarahemla'). Acts 11:22's 'the church which was in Jerusalem' is the same English construction and nothing more; the verse is about Barnabas being sent to Antioch and shares no other word.

Four words. The kingdom established in the hand of Solomon after an execution has nothing to do with a church established in a city, and 'established' is one of this book's commonest verbs. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

sharedText: their names were blotted out, that their names were not numbered among those of the righteous
reason: Adjudicated one chapter earlier, at Alma 5:57, where the same two clauses are argued against Psalm 69:28's KJV singletons 'blotted out of the book' and 'written with the righteous'. Alma 6:3 is the narrative performing what Alma 5:57 commanded, in the sermon's own words, and the row is recorded there as a recurrence. A reader arriving at 6:3 should be sent to 5:57; the blotting out of names is the sermon's one instruction whose execution the record reports.

reason: Genuinely apt and still not a link. Acts 13:44's 'the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God' is a congregation assembling to hear preaching, which is what Alma 6:5 describes, so the temptation is real. But every content word in the run is unavoidable for the sense, 'the word of God' is this book's constant phrase, and the two verses agree on nothing else — Acts 13:44 leads to the Jews' envy and Paul turning to the Gentiles. The verse's identifiable source is James 1:5, filed as a link on the much rarer 'liberal'.

reason: A six-word run of pure connective syntax; 'gather themselves together' is the KJV's ordinary phrase for an assembly and occurs across both testaments. Ezra 10:7's proclamation summoning the returned exiles to Jerusalem to put away foreign wives has no other contact with a church commanded to meet often for fasting and prayer. The fasting and prayer are Acts 14:23's and are recorded at the link at 6:1.

Worth an entry because the reversal is attractive and the evidence will not support it. The KJV has 'them that know not God' at 2 Thessalonians 1:8, where they are the objects of vengeance in flaming fire, and 'the Gentiles which know not God' at 1 Thessalonians 4:5 — so Alma 6:6, in which the church fasts and prays 'in behalf of the welfare of the souls of those who knew not God', looks like a deliberate answer to Paul's sentence of judgment. But the Book of Mormon's tense is past, which matches instead 1 Corinthians 1:21 and Galatians 4:8, where the phrase describes the addressees' own former state and carries no threat at all. Four verses, two tenses, and no distinctive word beyond the three; no source is identifiable and the reversal cannot be claimed.

Topographical boilerplate in a verse that is doing nothing but naming a place — 'the valley that was called Gideon'. Judges 18:28's valley by Bethrehob is a different valley in a different narrative; the shared words are the only way English says the thing.

Alma 6:8 is built of four 'according to' clauses in a row, which is why Romans 16:25 and Romans 1:4 both score here and why neither is a source. 'According to the revelation of the mystery' and 'according to the revelation of the truth of the word' share only the frame. The verse's real borrowings are the two rare phrases inside those clauses — 'the spirit of prophecy' with 'the testimony of Jesus', and 'the Son of God which should come' — both filed as links.
